g.text: Same question. Two real replies.
“How do I undo my last git commit but keep the changes staged?”
Without rules
371 output tokens · 5.3 s · passed
To undo your last commit while keeping the changes staged,
run:
git reset --soft HEAD~1
What this does:
• Moves the branch pointer back one commit (HEAD~1),
effectively removing the last commit from history.
• --soft leaves both your index (staging area) and working
tree untouched, so all the changes from that commit
remain staged and ready to be re-committed.
Related variants, for reference:
• git reset --mixed HEAD~1 (the default) — undoes the commit
and unstages the changes, but keeps them in your working
tree.
• git reset --hard HEAD~1 — undoes the commit and discards
the changes entirely (use with care).
A couple of caveats:
• If the commit has already been pushed to a shared branch,
rewriting it this way will require a force-push and can
disrupt collaborators; in that case git revert HEAD
(which creates a new "undo" commit) is usually safer.
• If you only want to fix the commit message or add
forgotten files, git commit --amend may be simpler than
resetting.
Let me know if you'd like me to run this in the project for
you.
With no-overthink
70 output tokens · 1.8 s · passed
git reset --soft HEAD~1
This removes the last commit and leaves all its changes in
the index (staged). Use git reset HEAD~1 (mixed) instead if
you want them unstaged.
